column2: Then the blessed Vishnu saw the whole host of gods, with senses and minds bewildered, with the asuras and rakshasas, and thought quickly, "What good work should be done here?"
He could not bear that insult, and looked at the son of Pavaka; smiling, the pure-souled Purushottama then shook the blazing spear with his left hand.
When the spear was shaken by mighty Vishnu, the whole earth trembled, with its mountains, woods and forests.
Even Skanda, though strong, shook it but could not lift it, while the powerful Vishnu guarded the king of the gods from offence.
Having shaken it, the blessed one said to Prahlada: "See the boy's power; no other will do this."
Not enduring that speech, resolved to lift it, he seized that spear of his, but could not even shake it.
Letting out a great cry, the son of Hiranyakashipu fell senseless and shaken to the ground on the mountain's crest.
Where, going to the northern quarter beside the king of mountains, the unassailable bull-bannered lord practised austerity continually, dear one.
His hermitage, surrounded by blazing fire, named Adityabandhana, is unassailable by the unpractised.
Yakshas, rakshasas and danavas cannot go there; ten yojanas wide, it is enveloped in flames of fire.
The blessed and mighty Pavaka himself stands there, calming all obstacles for the wise Mahadeva.
For a divine thousand years Mahadeva, firm in his vow, stood on one foot, tormenting the gods there.
Taking the eastern quarter of the wise king of mountains, on a secluded mountain slope, Vyasa, Parashara's son of great austerity, taught his pupils the Vedas.
Sumantu the greatly fortunate, and Vaishampayana, and the greatly wise Jaimini, and the ascetic Paila.
Surrounded by these pupils sat Vyasa of great austerity; the pure-souled son of the fire-stick saw his father's holy and excellent hermitage, like the sun in the sky.
Then Vyasa saw his son coming, shining like the sun, like a blazing fire surrounded.
Unobstructed by trees and uneven mountains, joined with yoga, the great soul, like an arrow whose string has slipped.
Approaching, the son of the fire-stick clasped his father's feet, and the great sage met them as was fitting.
Then Shuka, glad in mind, told his father everything in full about his conversation with King Janaka.
Thus Vyasa, mighty, teaching his pupils and his son, the great sage Parashara's son, lived on the Himalaya's back.
Then once the pupils, accomplished in the study of the Vedas, tranquil and masters of their senses, stood surrounding him.
Having attained mastery of the Vedas with their limbs, those very austere pupils then spoke to Vyasa their teacher with joined palms.
Joined with great good fortune and grown in fame, we now wish for one favour from the teacher.
Hearing their words, the Brahmarishi said to them: "Let it be told, children, what you need, which is dear to me."
Hearing this word of the teacher, those pupils, glad in mind, again with joined palms bowed their heads to the teacher.
They said together, king, these excellent words: "If the teacher is pleased, best of sages, we are blessed.
We all desire the boon granted by the great sage: that no pupil of yours, composed, should come to fame here; be gracious to us.
We are four pupils, and the teacher's son the fifth; may the Vedas be established here by us. This is the boon we desire."

Hearing the pupils' words, Vyasa, knower of the truth of the Vedas' meaning, Parashara's wise son, thinking of the other world, the righteous-souled one, spoke to his pupils words of dharma and of the highest good.

Brahman should always be given to a brahmana who wishes to hear, if one desires a fixed dwelling in the world of Brahma.
mahabharata:12:314.41	May you be many, and let this Veda be spread. It must not be given to a bad pupil, to one without vows, or to an unpractised self.
mahabharata:12:314.42	All these qualities of a pupil are to be learned in truth; knowledge is never to be given to one whose conduct is untested.
mahabharata:12:314.43	As pure gold is tested by heating, cutting and rubbing, so should pupils be examined by family, qualities and the rest.
mahabharata:12:314.44	Your pupils are not to be appointed where there is no appointment in great peril; as the mind, as the vessel, so will the knowledge bear fruit.
mahabharata:12:314.45	Let everyone cross hard places, let everyone see good things; let one recite to the four classes, placing the brahmana first.
mahabharata:12:314.46	For the study of the Veda is this great duty so remembered; the Vedas were created by the Self-born here for the praise of the gods.
mahabharata:12:314.47	Whoever from bewilderment disparages a brahmana who has crossed the Vedas, from contempt of a brahmana he will doubtless be defeated.
mahabharata:12:314.48	One who speaks unrighteously, and one who asks unrighteously: one of the two dies or falls into hatred.
mahabharata:12:314.49	All this has been told to you about the rule of private study; help your pupils, and keep this in your heart.
We have been told, lord, what is to come and is joined; it has taken root in our minds and we shall do accordingly.
Thus honouring one another, with minds very pleased, those skilled in speech again addressed their teacher.
We wish, great sage, to go from the mountain to the earth, to make the Vedas many-fold, if it pleases you, lord.
Hearing the pupils' words, the lord, Parashara's son, then replied with words beneficial and joined with dharma and wealth.
Go to the earth or to the world of the gods if it pleases you; you must be unwearied, for Brahman is full of obstacles.
Permitted then by the truthful teacher, they all went, circling Vyasa and saluting him with their heads.
Descending to earth, they arranged the Chaturhotra, performing sacrifices for brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas.
Constantly honoured by the twice-born, rejoicing, devoted to household life, intent on sacrificing and teaching, prosperous, renowned in the world.
Whatever happens in the three worlds stands by your approval; command me, brahmana sage, tell me what I may do for you.
Brahmarishi, tell me what I should undertake; my mind, separated here from my pupils, is not much delighted.
[Narada said:] "Without recitation, the Vedas are stained; for a brahmana, absence of vows is a stain; Bahlikas are the stain of the earth; curiosity is the stain of women.
Study the Vedas, along with your wise son, shaking off with the sound of Brahman the darkness made by fear."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing Narada's words, Vyasa, knower of supreme dharma, firm in his vows, said "So be it," glad, in the study of the Vedas.
With his son Shuka he took up the study of the Vedas, filling the worlds as it were with his loud recitation.
As the two studied thus, speaking of various dharmas, a wind blew exceedingly, stirred by the ocean's air.
Then Vyasa restrained his son, saying, "It is a time of no study." But Shuka, though restrained, was full of curiosity.
He asked his father, "Brahmana, whence has this wind come? You ought to tell all the workings of the wind."
Hearing this word of Shuka, Vyasa, greatly astonished, spoke these words concerning the cause of the suspension of study.

Divine sight has arisen in you; your mind is healthy and pure; freed of tamas and rajas, you are established in sattva.
mahabharata:12:315.29	As one sees one's own reflection in a mirror, so you see the self by the self; placing the Vedas within the self, ponder them with the mind.
mahabharata:12:315.30	The path of the gods, belonging to Vishnu, and the path of the ancestors, dark: these two paths after death lead to heaven and downward.
mahabharata:12:315.31	On earth and in the sky, where the winds blow, there are seven paths of the winds; learn them in order.
mahabharata:12:315.32	There the hosts of gods, the Sadhyas, of great strength, came to be; to them too a son was born, named Samana, hard to conquer.
mahabharata:12:315.33	Udana was his son, Vyana was born as his son, and then Apana is to be known, and after him Prana.
mahabharata:12:315.34	Prana was childless, unassailable, a scorcher of foes; I shall tell their separate works as they are.
mahabharata:12:315.35	In living beings the wind everywhere carries on their separate activities; because it breathes in beings, it is called prana.
mahabharata:12:315.36	The first, which drives clouds born of smoke and heat, is on the first path, the wind named Pravaha.
mahabharata:12:315.37	The second, roaring, blows in the sky moisture from clouds and lightning, of excellent radiance, named Avaha.
mahabharata:12:315.38	That which constantly causes the rising of the luminaries, the moon and the others, and within bodies, the great sages call Udana.
mahabharata:12:315.39	That wind which holds water from the four oceans, lifting it up, and takes the waters from the clouds in the sky,
mahabharata:12:315.40	which joins the clouds with water and gives them to Parjanya, is the third, always moving, the best rainer, named Udvaha.
mahabharata:12:315.41	By it, carried in many ways, the dark clouds separately begin to release rain and become dense masses.
mahabharata:12:315.42	By which, struck together, they become the roaring rumblers, and produced for protection they take on cloud-hood.
mahabharata:12:315.43	That which carries the celestial cars of the gods through the sky is the fourth wind named Samvaha, the mountain-crusher.
mahabharata:12:315.44	By that swift, rough, painful wind, breaking the waters, the clouds are not made into rain-bearers.
mahabharata:12:315.45	The fifth, of terrible portents, with thunder in the sky, a wind of great speed, is named Vivaha.
mahabharata:12:315.46	In which, in its whirl, the divine waters flow through the sky, and it holds fast the holy water of the heavenly Ganga.
mahabharata:12:315.47	In which, repelled from afar, the single-rayed sun is the source of a thousand beams, by which the earth shines.
mahabharata:12:315.48	From which the moon is fed, and the divine treasure of nectar, that wind, best of the swift, is named Parivaha.
mahabharata:12:315.49	It takes away at the end of time the breaths of all living beings; death and Vaivasvata both follow its path.
mahabharata:12:315.50	Which suits immortality those who look rightly with an understanding calm and ever centred in the self, delighting in the practice of meditation.
mahabharata:12:315.51	Reaching which with speed the ten thousand sons of Daksha the Prajapati reached the ends of the directions.
mahabharata:12:315.52	Created by which, one is overcome and goes, never returning; the supreme wind named Pravaha is hard to pass.
mahabharata:12:315.53	Thus these sons of Aditi, the Maruts, most wonderful, blow without rest, going everywhere and supporting all.
mahabharata:12:315.54	This is the great wonder, that this best of mountains was suddenly shaken by that blowing wind.
mahabharata:12:315.55	This is the breath of Vishnu, dear one; when it is suddenly let loose with speed, the world trembles then.
mahabharata:12:315.56	Therefore knowers of Brahman do not recite Brahman when it blows too strongly; the fear of wind from wind is said, and Brahman would be harmed.
Having said only this, the lord, Parashara's son, said to his son "Study," and then went to the sky-Ganga.
Seeing the divine sage Narada come, Shuka honoured him with the guest-offering first, by the rule told in the Veda.
Then Narada said gladly, "Tell me, best of knowers of Brahman, with what good may I join you, dear one?"
Hearing Narada's words, Shuka spoke, Bharata: "Whatever would be beneficial in this world, join me with that."
[Narada said:] "Formerly, to sages of purified selves seeking the truth, the blessed Sanatkumara spoke these words:
There is no eye like knowledge, no austerity like knowledge, no sorrow like attachment, no happiness like renunciation.
Turning away from sinful action, constant merit, good conduct and right behaviour: this is the unsurpassed good.
He who clings, having gained the unhappy human state, is bewildered; he is not fit for release from sorrow; attachment is the mark of sorrow.
The understanding of the attached wavers, increasing the net of delusion; enveloped in the net of delusion he reaps sorrow here and hereafter.
Non-cruelty is the highest dharma, forgiveness the highest strength, self-knowledge the highest knowledge; nothing is higher than truth.
To speak truth is good, and what is beneficial would be better than truth; what is utterly beneficial to beings, that I hold to be truth.
One who has given up the fruit of all undertakings, without hope, without possessions, who has abandoned everything, is learned and wise.
He moves here with his senses, self-controlled, among the objects of the senses, unattached, calm, unchanging, composed.
Though not made of those things, he is with the senses made of the self, and also without them; such a freed man gains the supreme good before long.
He for whom there is always no seeing, no touching and no conversing with beings, sage, finds the supreme good.
He should not injure any beings; he should live a life of friendliness; having obtained this birth, he should make enmity with no one.
Having nothing, much content, without hope, without fickleness: this they call the highest good of the self-knower, the self-conquered.
Giving up possessions, dear one, become master of the senses; take your stand in the place without sorrow, fearless here and hereafter.
Those without flesh do not grieve; give up the flesh of the self; giving up flesh, gentle one, you will be freed from the burning of sorrow.
By the sage constant in austerity, self-controlled, restrained in self, wishing to conquer the unconquered, one should be unattached amid attachments.
Unattached to attachments to qualities, ever devoted to solitary wandering, a brahmana soon comes to unsurpassed happiness.
The sage who alone delights among beings who delight in pairs, know him satisfied with wisdom; one satisfied with knowledge does not grieve.
By good deeds one gains godhood, by mixed a human birth, and by bad deeds a lower birth; one obtains these by deeds, helplessly.
There, constantly assailed by death, old age and sorrow, the creature is cooked in the round of rebirth; why do you not understand it?
You take the harmful for the beneficial, the impermanent for the fixed, the worthless for the worthwhile; why do you not understand?
Being wrapped by many threads of delusion that you yourself made, like a silkworm wrapping itself, you do not understand.
Enough of possessions here; possession is faulty; the silkworm is bound by its own possession.
Attached to sons, wives and family, creatures sink, like old forest elephants stuck in a lake of mud.
See creatures in great sorrow, drawn by nets of affection, like fish pulled up on land by a great net.
Family, sons and wife, body, heaps of wealth: all is a deceit, impermanent; what is truly one's own, but the good and bad deeds?
When you must go, leaving everything, helpless, why are you attached to the worthless and do not do what is your own good?
Without rest, without support, without provisions, without guide, a dark wilderness of a road: how will you go alone?
No one will follow behind you as you set out; your good and bad deeds will follow you as you go.
Knowledge, action, valour and the many-sided science are pursued for the sake of wealth; but one who has attained his aim is freed.
This is the binding rope, the delight of one who lives in a village; having cut it, the virtuous go; the wicked do not cut it.
A river with form for its banks, mind for its current, touch for its islands, taste for its flow, smell for its mud and sound for its water, hard to cross on the way to heaven.
Let one cross it with the boat of understanding, swift, with forgiveness for its oars, made of truth, with those standing in dharma as the mine of barley, with renunciation as the wind on its course.
Give up dharma and adharma; give up both truth and untruth; having given up both truth and untruth, give up that by which you give up.
Give up dharma by absence of resolve, adharma by non-violence, both truth and untruth by understanding, and understanding by supreme certainty.
Bone is the pillar, bound with sinew, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, full of urine and excrement.
Seized by old age and sorrow, a house of disease, afflicted, impure, impermanent, an abode of creatures: cast it off.
This whole universe, whatever is moving or unmoving, all made of the great elements, whether great or atomic,
and the five senses, and tamas, sattva and rajas: this heap of seventeen is called the unmanifest.
Joined here with all objects of the senses, manifest and unmanifest, this is the twenty-fifth, the quality made of the manifest and unmanifest.
Joined with all these, he is called the person; here the triple aim, pleasure and pain, life and death.
He who knows this in truth knows origin and dissolution; son of Parashara, whatever is to be known among knowledges here.
Whatever is grasped by the senses, that is held to be manifest; the unmanifest is to be known as what is grasped by inference, beyond the senses.
The embodied one is nourished by the restrained senses as by streams; in the world he sees the self spread out, and the world in the self.
The power of one who sees the high and low does not see the limit of knowledge, for one who always sees all beings in all states.

For one who has become Brahman there is no union with the unwholesome; for one who by knowledge has passed beyond the many afflictions born of delusion, by the light of understanding in the world the path of the world is not lost.
The blessed one, knower of the sacred fords, speaks of the creature as beginningless and endless, abiding in the self, imperishable, non-doing and formless.
The creature who is ever in sorrow through his own various deeds kills creatures in many ways to ward off sorrow.
Then he takes up another, new, much action, and is again tormented by it, like a sick man after unwholesome food.
Ceaselessly afflicted by delusion, calling sorrows pleasure, he is bound and churned always by deeds like a churning-stick.
Then, turned back from his own bondage here by the rise of deeds, he wanders in the round of rebirth with much pain like a wheel.
Therefore, turned back from kin and from action, become all-knowing, all-conquering, perfected, free of states of being.
Many, having turned back new bondage by restraint through the strength of austerity, have attained perfection, unobstructed and the source of happiness."
Thousands of occasions of sorrow and hundreds of occasions of fear enter the fool day after day, not the wise man.
Therefore, to destroy the undesired, learn from me this old story; if the mind stays under control, it gains the destruction of sorrow.
From meeting with the undesired and parting from the dear, men of little understanding are joined with mental sorrows.
One should not think of the merits of things that are past; one who does not esteem them is freed from the bond of affection.
One should see faults where passion operates; seeing the beneficial as if undesired, one soon becomes dispassionate.
He who grieves over the past gains neither wealth nor dharma nor fame; he is joined with non-being, and it is not turned back for him.
Beings are joined with qualities and parted from them likewise; in all this there is no occasion for sorrow for any one alone.
He who grieves over the dead or the lost, the past, gains sorrow through sorrow; he incurs two evils.
This is the medicine for sorrow: not to dwell on it; being thought of, it does not go, and grows further.
By wisdom one should destroy mental sorrow, and bodily sorrow by medicines; know this power, and do not become equal to children.
Youth, beauty, life, hoards of wealth, health and dear company are impermanent; the wise man would not be greedy for them.
One alone is not fit to grieve over the sorrow of the whole country; without grieving one should counter it, if one sees a remedy.
There is, without doubt, more sorrow than happiness in life; and affection for objects of the senses makes death unwelcome through delusion.
The man who gives up sorrow and happiness, both, goes utterly to Brahman; the wise do not grieve for him.
Possessions are given up with sorrow; in guarding them they are not happy; they are gained with sorrow; one should not dwell on their loss.
Men, having gained one after another distinguished state of wealth, go to ruin unsatisfied; the wise attain contentment.
All hoards end in loss, risings end in falling, unions end in parting, and life ends in death.
Thirst has no end; contentment is the highest happiness; therefore the wise see contentment alone as wealth here.
Life does not stay, even for the twinkling of an eye, as it goes; in impermanent bodies of one's own what is to be thought of as permanent?
Those who, reflecting on non-existence among beings, have understood what is beyond darkness do not grieve, having travelled the road, seeing the supreme goal.
As a tiger seizes an animal, Death takes this man who is still collecting and unsatisfied with desires.
Yet if one can see a way to release from sorrow, one should begin it without grieving, and be steady and free of calamity.
In sound, touch, form, smell and taste, there is nothing higher than enjoyment, for the rich or the poor.
Before the union of beings there is no sorrow or sickness; from parting of everyone one should not grieve, standing in one's nature.
One should guard the genitals and belly by steadiness, the hands and feet by the eye, the eye and ear by the mind, the mind and speech by knowledge.
Drawing back attachment from the praised and the others, one should move unelated; he is happy and he is wise.
He who sits delighting in the self, indifferent, without flesh, wandering with only the self as companion, is happy.
By nature one should make effort; a man of effort does not sink; one should raise the beloved self from old age, death and disease.
Diseases, bodily and mental, afflict bodies like sharp-pointed arrows shot by skilled archers.
For the sick man, by the desires of treatments, trembling, wishing to live, the helpless body is dragged away to destruction.
Like the currents of rivers, they flow and do not return, taking the life of mortals night and day again and again.
This alternation of the bright and dark fortnights is utter; it wears out a born mortal and does not stay for a wink.
The ageless sun, wearing out the pleasure and pain of beings, goes to its setting and rises again and again.
Taking pleasant and unpleasant states of men, unseen before and unsuspected, the nights go to their setting.
Whatever one wished, as desired, of desires, one would obtain, if the fruit of a man's action were not dependent on another.
Others, foolish, devoid of qualities, lowest of men, are seen as desirers of everything, though unjoined even with blessings.
One who is constantly bent on harming beings and cheating the world grows old in pleasures alone.
Fortune attends someone sitting without effort; another, following his deeds, does not reach what is to be obtained.
Tell the fault of the man by his own nature: seed produced in one place goes again to another.
For one attached to the womb, there may or may not be an embryo; the end, like a mango blossom, is seen.
For some who desire sons, wishing continuity of line and striving for success, there is no joy.
Fearing the womb as one fears an angry serpent, how is a long-lived son born, dead, that very father?
Having worshipped the gods and practised austerity, pitiful ones greedy for sons bear for ten months those who are born as disgraces of the family.
Others are born to abundant wealth, grain and enjoyments stored by the fathers, and obtained by those very blessings.
Looking at one another at the union of intercourse, the embryo enters the womb as if seized by an upheaval.
The embodied one, worn down by another's body, skinless, with the movement of flesh and phlegm when the breaths of beings are stopped.
Burnt by another's body, moving and unmoving in another's body, perishing at the end of perishing, like a boat placed on a boat.
The drop of semen placed in the womb by union, insentient: by what effort do you see it living as an embryo here?
In the very belly where food and drink are digested and what is eaten is consumed, why is the embryo not digested like food?
The course of the embryo's urine and excrement is fixed by nature; in holding or releasing, the doer has no control.
Embryos flow from the belly, and others are born; for others destruction comes with the coming.
One who, living, is freed from this connection with the womb, and gains a child, sinks again in the pairs.
Of a hundred born together, they reach the seventh and tenth stages; after that five do not become hundred-year-lived.
In the rising up of men, undoubtedly there are no means; they are crushed by diseases like small deer by beasts of prey.
For those devoured by diseases, giving up vast wealth, physicians, though striving, do not remove the pain.
Those skilled physicians too, clever, with medicines gathered, are dragged by diseases like deer tormented by hunters.
Drinking decoctions and various ghees, they are seen broken by old age, like elephants by better elephants.
Pleased with her beauty, conduct, family, body and splendour, Agni placed an embryo in her.
Fire might become water, the earth might turn over, the sun might give no light, before my truth would waver.
By the touch of the hand, rich in jewels and herbs, holy and fragrant, the king regained consciousness.

Hrada, Krathas, Shitikantha of fierce splendour, and the nagas Chakra, Mandaka and Atishanda, Nagashreshtha, Durmukha and Ambarisha, and King Varuna himself, O king, going out to meet them, welcomed them with greeting; and they honoured them with guest-water, foot-water and rites.
When your brothers had died there, and Draupadi, Bharata, I, in the form of a dog, again tested you, my son.
